findings.title: New abstract method order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: CryptoProvider adds `int order();` without a `default` implementation. Any third-party or downstream implementation of CryptoProvider that compiled against the old interface will fail at runtime with AbstractMethodError and will fail to compile against the new interface. For a service-loaded SPI this is a breaking contract change. It should be a `default` method (e.g. `default int order() { return 0; }`) so old providers keep working and the new AuthzClientCryptoProvider with order 100 stays lowest priority.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns unrelated KeyStore provider
findings.body: AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, typically the SUN/JDK provider, not a BouncyCastle provider. Callers use this method to obtain the BC/BCCFIPS provider for BC-specific operations. Returning an arbitrary JDK provider is misleading and will cause ClassCast or NoSuchAlgorithm failures when BC-specific behavior is expected. Like WildFlyElytronProvider it should return null or throw UnsupportedOperationException if no BC provider is available.

findings.title: Authz client crypto provider cannot sign or load keys
findings.body: AuthzClientCryptoProvider throws UnsupportedOperationException from getSignature, getKeyFactory, getKeyPairGen, createECParams, getCertificateUtils, getPemUtils and others. The authz-client needs those for common paths such as private_key_jwt client authentication, JWKS parsing and JWT verification via CryptoIntegration.getProvider(). With only this provider on the classpath, AuthzClient.create() now succeeds in CryptoIntegration.init but fails later with confusing UOE instead of working. Those methods should delegate to the default JCA (e.g. Signature.getInstance without provider, KeyFactory.getInstance) rather than unconditionally throwing.

findings.title: Test reuses one P-256 key for ES384/ES512 and only round-trips
findings.body: ECDSAAlgorithmTest generates a single default EC KeyPair (P-256) in the constructor and reuses it for ES256, ES384 and ES512, and only checks asn1->concat->DER->concat round-trip equality. It never verifies the signature, never exercises real P-384/P-521 key sizes, and padding/truncation bugs in integerToBytes for the larger signLength values (e.g. left-padding a 32-byte value to 48/66 bytes) still round-trip successfully. The test therefore cannot catch incorrect length handling or interop failures with JCA verifiers.
